summary: The direct object — the thing you eat, drink, cook, buy, want or like — is in the accusative (النَّصْب). With the article it ends in -a: أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ; without the article in -an, written with an extra alif: أَشْرَبُ شَايًا (except after ة and after ـاء: قَهْوَةً، مَاءً). The verb takes its object directly, with no preposition, and the object normally follows the verb. Feminine plurals in -āt take -i / -in instead (أَشْتَرِي تُفَّاحَاتٍ), diptotes take -a without tanwīn (أَشْتَرِي فَوَاكِهَ), duals end in -ayni (آكُلُ بَيْضَتَيْنِ). For things in general Arabic uses the article: أُحِبُّ الشَّايَ = I like tea; the indefinite means “a / some”: أُرِيدُ شَايًا = I’d like (some) tea. A pronoun object is a suffix on the verb (أُحِبُّكَ, “I love you”) — a preview here. Objects with prepositions and the indirect object (“to whom”) come later (lessons 11–13 and the core lesson on two objects).

blocks.caption: Subject → object: -u becomes -a, -un becomes -an. The -āt plural uses -i / -in, a diptote has no tanwīn, the dual has -ayni.

blocks.title: Who does it: -u. What is affected: -a.
blocks.text: الْوَلَدُ يَأْكُلُ الْخُبْزَ — the boy (-u) eats the bread (-a). The endings, not the order, tell you who does what: يَأْكُلُ الْخُبْزَ الْوَلَدُ is still “the boy eats the bread”.

blocks.title: The extra alif of -an.
blocks.text: خُبْزًا، شَايًا، لَحْمًا — with alif. No alif after ة (قَهْوَةً، سَلَطَةً) and after ـاء (مَاءً، عَشَاءً، غَدَاءً). شَيْء puts its hamza on a seat: شَيْئًا.

items.title: the + noun = in general / the one we know

blocks.caption: A preview: the same endings as the possessives (كِتَابُكَ), except “me”: -nī on verbs, -ī on nouns.

blocks.title: “Them” for things is -hā.
blocks.text: Non-human plurals are feminine singular for agreement, so “I buy them (the apples)” is أَشْتَرِيهَا, not *أَشْتَرِيهِمْ. ـهُمْ is for people: أُحِبُّهُمْ (I love them).

Later: verbs that take their object with a preposition (to wait for, to look at), the indirect object (to give someone something) and the genitive after prepositions come in lessons 11–13 and in the core lesson on two objects.

askYourself: Is the noun the thing that is eaten, drunk, cooked, bought, wanted or liked? → it is the object → accusative.
Does it have the article? → -a (الشَّايَ); no article → -an (شَايًا).
Does it end in ة or ـاء? → -an without the extra alif (قَهْوَةً، مَاءً).
Is it a feminine plural in -āt? → -i / -in (تُفَّاحَاتٍ). A diptote (فَوَاكِه)? → -a, never tanwīn. A dual? → -ayni.
Is the subject a noun too? → the subject keeps -u: الْبِنْتُ تَأْكُلُ تُفَّاحَةً.
Is the object a pronoun (me, you, it)? → a suffix on the verb: أُحِبُّكَ.

traps: *أَشْرَبُ الشَّايُ is wrong: the object never keeps -u.
The article and tanwīn never go together: الشَّايَ or شَايًا, never *الشَّايًا.
No extra alif after ة: قَهْوَةً, not *قَهْوَةًا.
Sound feminine plurals have no -a: أَشْتَرِي تُفَّاحَاتٍ (-in), not *تُفَّاحَاتًا.
In عِنْدِي خُبْزٌ the bread is the subject (“at me is bread”), so it stays nominative — not an object (lesson 6).
After a number the counted noun is not the object: ثَلَاثَ تُفَّاحَاتٍ — the number takes the object case, the noun is genitive.

quiz.why: The object is accusative: -a with the article.
Indefinite object: -an; after ـاء no extra alif.
-an on ة, without alif; the article and tanwīn never go together.

quiz.q: “I’m buying three apples” — the form of تُفَّاحَات after ثَلَاثَ?
quiz.why: After 3–10 the counted noun is genitive plural; and -āt plurals never take -an.
Things in general take the article in Arabic.
The object “me” is the suffix -nī on a verb (-ī is for nouns: كِتَابِي).

seeAlso.note: German shows the accusative on the article, and only in the masculine (den Tee, einen Apfel; die Milch stays die); Arabic changes the ending of every noun (-a / -an).
Hebrew has no case endings: before a definite object it puts אֶת (אֲנִי שׁוֹתֶה אֶת הַקָּפֶה), an indefinite object gets nothing — Arabic marks both with the ending.
Chinese shows the object only by its place after the verb (我喝茶); nothing on the noun changes.
The three cases: the nominative (subject) was lesson 4; the genitive after prepositions comes in lesson 11.

notes.text: German marks the accusative only on the article, and only in the masculine (den Tee, einen Apfel); Arabic marks every object on the noun itself: الشَّايَ / شَايًا.
Greek marks the object on the article and the ending (τον καφέ); Arabic only on the ending, but for every noun: الشَّايَ / شَايًا.
Turkish adds -(y)ı only to a definite object (çayı içiyorum) and leaves an indefinite one bare (çay içiyorum); Arabic marks every object: الشَّايَ / شَايًا.
Russian is the closest: the ending changes (воду, кашу); Arabic does it with -a / -an on every noun.
Spanish nouns do not change as objects (bebo té) — only people get a (veo a Juan); Arabic marks every object with -a / -an.
English shows the object only by its place after the verb; Arabic marks it on the noun (-a / -an), so the order can change without changing who does what.
French shows the object by its place, and puts object pronouns before the verb (je le mange); Arabic marks the noun with -a / -an and attaches object pronouns after the verb (آكُلُهُ).
Hindi marks some objects with को (mostly people and definite things); Arabic marks every object with an ending.
Persian marks a definite object with -rā (چای را می‌خورم) and leaves an indefinite one bare; Arabic marks both: الشَّايَ / شَايًا.
Marathi marks some objects with -ला (people, definite things); Arabic marks every object with -a / -an.
Japanese marks the object with を after the noun (お茶を飲む) and puts the verb last; Arabic changes the noun’s ending and puts the verb first or in the middle.
Korean 을 / 를 after the noun (차를 마셔요) does the job of the Arabic ending -a.
Finnish chooses between the accusative and the partitive (luen kirjan / luen kirjaa); Arabic has one object case for every object.
Hungarian also marks every object, definite or not (kávét iszom, a kávét iszom); Arabic does it with -a / -an.

Swahili nouns do not change as objects; an object prefix inside the verb can stand for them (nimekinunua, I have bought it). Arabic marks the object noun with -a / -an and attaches object pronouns as endings (أَشْتَرِيهِ).
Luganda nouns do not change as objects, and an object prefix can sit inside the verb; Arabic marks the noun with -a / -an and attaches object pronouns as endings (أَشْتَرِيهِ).
Vietnamese shows the object only by its place after the verb (tôi uống trà); Arabic marks it on the noun: أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ.
Inuktitut marks the subject of a transitive verb (ergative) rather than the object, and puts an indefinite object in the -mik case; Arabic always marks the object with the accusative -a / -an.
